Face to Face. Canadian soldier Pvt. Patrick Cloutier and Anishinaabe Mohawk warrior Brad Larocque stare each other down during the Oka Crisis. Quebec, Canada. 1990

Face to Face is a photograph of Canadian Private Patrick Cloutier and Anishinaabe Mohawk warrior Brad Larocque staring each other down during the Oka Crisis. It was taken on Sept. 1, 1990 by Shaney Komulainen, and has become one of Canada's most famous images.

The Oka Crisis was a 78-day standoff (11 July–26 September 1990) between Mohawk protesters, police, and army. At the heart of the crisis was the proposed expansion of a golf course and development of condominiums on disputed land that included a Mohawk burial ground.

There was a long history behind the crisis at Oka; since the 18th century the Mohawk had been pressing the government to recognize their right to land in the area, but their requests had been largely ignored. In 1961, a nine-hole golf course was built on land that had been claimed by the Mohawk of the Kanesatake reserve. Despite protests that the land included a burial ground, the Mohawk claim was rejected and the golf course was built. In 1989, the mayor of Oka announced that the golf course would be expanded to 18 holes and condos would be built.

In order to halt the development, Mohawk protesters constructed barricades, blocking access to the area. Mohawk warriors from two other reserves—Kahnawake and Akwesasne—joined the protest, as did protesters from across Canada and the US. After two injunctions to remove the roadblock were ignored, the mayor of Oka asked the provincial police force, the Sûreté du Québec (SQ), to intervene. On the morning of 11 July 1990 the SQ attacked the barricade, using tear gas and concussion grenades to create confusion. During the brief gunfight that followed, SQ Corporal Marcel Lemay was killed and the SQ retreated. On August 20 about 800 members of the Royal 22nd Regiment (the “Van Doos”) took over from the SQ and overtook the barricades at Kahnawake and Kanesatake and then assumed a position only metres from the final barricade. The Mohawk continued their protest until September 26, 1990, when they surrendered to the army. Several were detained by the military and a number were later charged by the SQ. Five were convicted of crimes including assualt and theft, although only one served time in jail.

The golf course expansion which had originally triggered the crisis was cancelled. The Oka Crisis galvanized, throughout Canada, a subsequent process of developing a First Nations Policing Policy to try to prevent future such events.
